catalog_quote: The accent in Madimadi was more varied in position, but it was conditioned and not of direct phonemic significance. ... Primary stress occurs on the first syllable in words of two syllables ... In words of three or more syllables the primary stress was on the first syllable in the following circumstances: before single velar and labial consonants, g, ŋ, b, m, w; before most clusters, e.g. ŋg, lw, nm, ... and rb; more rarely before mb, ..., rg and lg, where there was some hesitation. ... All single consonants other than labials and velars, as well as vowels in hiatus, whenever they began the second syllable, attracted the main accent into the second syllable. A weak secondary accent ... remained on the first syllable ... There were only a few isolated exceptions to this rule, particularly when the optional glide -w- began the second syllable. audit.recode_to: Split by lect: keep Wembawemba (StressTyp2 unit) as fixed-strict initial (initial stress, word domain, clitics -gad(a)/-min unaccented) sourced to Hercus 1986 pp.21-22; move the Madimadi/Mathi-Mathi reading (onset- and, per PL 628 p.75, closed-syllable/diphthong-conditioned first-or-second syllable stress; WALS mdm 'Left-edge: first or second') to a separate dialect-level record madh1244 so its weight-sensitive tier quote no longer sits under a 'fixed-strict' kind.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: both the Wembawemba deciding quote (pp.21-22) and the Madimadi tier quote (pp.115-116, 112, 155) are verbatim in the PL B-77 PDF we hold at the stated pages. Source quality: Hercus 1986 is a salvage grammar sketch but is the primary and only description of Wembawemba accentuation; Glottolog lists nothing else for west2443, and the newly downloaded PL 628 (Blake, Hercus, Morey & Ryan 2011, open access, states again that Wemba-Wemba 'invariably had a heavy stress accent on the first syllable' (p.73), so the catalog's classification fixed-strict initial for the Wembawemba unit is secure. The problem is identity, already flagged in the record's idn field: Glottolog west2443 'Western Victoria' lumps Wembawemba and Madhi Madhi (madh1244, ISO dmd, WALS mdm), and the record carries classification fixed-strict/rule=initial (Wembawemba, from StressTyp2

sources.quote: "The principal accent of every Wembawemba word is a strong stress accent which falls on the first syllable." (p. 21). Continuing, same section: "In words of three or four syllables, while the first syllable bears the main accent, the third syllable bears a secondary accent ..." (p. 21) and "In words of five or more syllables the fourth syllable usually has a very strong secondary stress, and the sixth syllable again has a subsidiary secondary stress ..." (p. 22).

sources.quote: p.73: 'The system of accentuation of Mathi-Mathi differed considerably from the accentuation of Werkaya and Wemba-Wemba, which invariably had a heavy stress accent on the first syllable.' pp.74-75 restate Hercus 1986 (monosyllables accented; disyllables initial; 3+ syllables initial before single k ng p m w and most clusters; coronal single onsets and hiatus attract main accent to 2nd syllable; nd, lp -> 2nd; rrk mb nd lk hesitation) and ADD: 'If the second syllable was heavy, i.e. if it was a closed syllable or contained a diphthong it also tended to attract the stress accent ... not an absol
sources.locator: ch.3 sec. 3.1.6 Accentuation, 3.1.7 Position of the accent, 3.1.8 'The Mathi-Mathi accentuation system from a wider perspective', printed pp.73-78
sources.note: Full 2011 grammar of Mathi-Mathi by Hercus and colleagues; restates the 1986 accent rules and adds a heavy-second-syllable (closed/diphthong) condition, so the Madimadi tier fields what counts as heavy='onset-or-other' / 'no coda weight' need re-reading; also confirms Wemba-Wemba invariable initial stress.
